blocks.content: A resource limit sets the maximum a container is ever allowed to consume, enforced by the exact same cgroups mechanism covered in the Docker Internals module, just configured through Kubernetes instead of a raw Docker flag.

Where a request (covered in the previous topic) is a guaranteed minimum, a limit is the opposite, the absolute maximum a container is permitted to use, regardless of how much is actually available on the node.

blocks.alt: A hard ceiling, no matter how much capacity the node actually has free

blocks.content: This is not a Kubernetes-invented mechanism, Kubernetes resource limits are implemented using exactly the same cgroups feature covered in full mechanical detail in the Docker Internals module, Kubernetes is simply configuring them on your behalf.

blocks.alt: The exact same cgroups mechanism already covered, just configured by Kubernetes

blocks.content: If a container tries to use more CPU than its limit allows, it is throttled, slowed down, but it keeps running, this is a soft, recoverable consequence, not a termination.

blocks.alt: Slowed down, not killed, a soft, recoverable consequence

blocks.content: Memory behaves very differently, exceeding a memory limit results in the container being OOMKilled, exactly the mechanism covered in the Docker Performance module's Resource Limits topic, a hard termination, not a gradual slowdown.

blocks.alt: A hard kill, not a slowdown, exactly as covered for Docker containers

blocks.content: Put together, requests and limits define a range: the guaranteed minimum a container can count on, and the hard maximum it is never allowed to exceed, most production Pods declare both, not just one or the other.

blocks.alt: A guaranteed floor and a hard ceiling, defining the full range together

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: A resource limit is the hard maximum a container can use, enforced by the same cgroups mechanism covered in the Docker Internals module.
Exceeding a CPU limit throttles the container, exceeding a memory limit gets it OOMKilled outright, a genuinely important asymmetry covered in full in the next two topics.
